If the diagonals of a square decrease at a rate of $3\sqrt{2}\text{ m}\text{/min}$, at what rate is the perimeter decreasing?

feedback.problem:
The sides (in feet) of a square are increasing. At a particular moment, the rate of increase of the area of the square is numerically equal to seven times the rate of increase of the diagonals. What is the length $h$ of the diagonal of the square at that moment?

$h=$
{{field-1}} $\text{ft}$
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

The given information tells us that $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=7\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}$, so replacing $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ in the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}7\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} & =h\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ 7\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} & =h\cancel{\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}} \\ 7 & =h.\end{aligned}
$$

So at that particular moment, we have that the length of the diagonals of the square is $7\,\text{ ft}.$
